options: keep their face in mind while we watch.
same here. this story is about exactly that.
that’s honest. the story might show you.

steps.line: Long ago in Varanasi, at dawn, the young Hindu teacher Shankara walked down to bathe in the holy river Ganga, his students behind him.
steps.label: a traditional story

steps.line: A man came toward them with four dogs. The harsh caste rules of that time pushed his people to the edges, and told others not to touch them.
Move aside, Shankara told him. Get out of the way.

steps.q: The man doesn’t move. He asks Shankara a question. What do you think he asks?
o: “Why are you so rude to me?”
steps.why: He takes Shankara’s own teaching and hands it back: if the self in every person is one, who is moving away from whom?

steps.line: Move what? he asked. My body from yours, or the self in me from the self in you? The sun shines the same in the Ganga and my clay pot.

steps.q: Why did the question stop Shankara in his tracks?
o: He’d lost an argument in public
He was afraid of the four dogs
His own teaching had caught him out
steps.why: Shankara taught that the deepest self is one in all. The man caught him not living it, and Shankara knew it.

steps.line: Shankara bowed low before the man. Whoever truly sees this, he said, outcaste or priest, is my teacher. In many tellings, the man was the god Shiva.

steps.pre: Namaste is two Sanskrit words. Namas means a bow. Te means
steps.why: To you. A bow to you. “The light in me honors the light in you” is a modern reading, not a translation.

steps.line: Today, across India and Nepal, palms together and namaste is how people greet an aunt, a neighbor, a guest at the door.
steps.label: today

steps.q: In many tellings the man was Shiva. And the four dogs?
steps.why: The four Vedas, the oldest Hindu scriptures, walking at the heels of the man Shankara pushed aside. Shankara did have four famous students, which makes it sharper.

say: here’s what i love. shankara taught that one sacred self lives in every person. so a bow isn’t to someone’s job, caste or mood. it’s to that.
and the story shows how easy it is to know this and forget it on a busy morning. namaste, said and meant, is how you remember.

steps.q: From this story, when does a namaste really mean what it says?
o: When your palms are pressed just right
When it’s for someone you’d walk past
When it’s for elders and teachers
steps.why: The gesture is simple. The story’s test is who you bow to, and whether the bow is real.

today.say: today, really greet one person you usually walk past: the cleaner, the driver, the neighbor. a namaste, a nod, a real hello. mean the bow.
options: lovely. that’s shankara’s lesson, carried out the door.
that counts. looking is half of it.

card.keepWhy: A bow to you. Mean it.
sources: Traditional account of Adi Shankara and the chandala at Kashi (Varanasi), told in the hagiographies (e.g. Madhava-Vidyaranya’s Shankara Digvijaya, canto 6) and as the setting of the hymn Manisha Panchakam, attributed to Shankara.

Manisha Panchakam, opening verse: the question whether Shankara wants the body (made of food) to move from the body, or consciousness from consciousness; the sun reflected the same in the Ganga and in water in an outcaste’s pot; refrain that whoever has this vision is his guru, be he chandala or Brahmin.
namaste: Sanskrit namas (bow, reverence) + te (to you). Monier-Williams, Sanskrit-English Dictionary, s.v. namas.
